## Introduction

### Data Set 1: Diabetic Patient Hospital Readmission in the US

**Background & Motivation:**

Approximately 40 million Americans (12.5% of the population) are currently diagnosed with the metabolic disorder diabetes mellitus, the vast majority of which (90-95%) are diagnosed with type 2 [@cdc_type2_diabetes]. Type 2 diabetes is characterized by insulin resistant cells, driving the pancreas into overdrive and inducing hyperglycemia and high blood pressure, both of which can lead to a number of severe health issues, including blindness, kidney disease, and cardiovascular events[@cdc_type2_diabetes] [@fang2021trends].

As such, diabetes treatment has rapidly become a pressing public health issue, with particular attention paid to reducing the risk of comorbidities via rigorous glycemic, blood-pressure, and lipid management [@fang2021trends].

Since the 1980s, glycated hemoglobin of hemogolbin A1c (HbA1c) has been used in clinical testing to measure a patient's blood glucose levels across 90 days. HbA1c is a variant of hemoglobin (the oxygen binding protein abundant in red blood cells), in which glucose is conjugated to the beta chain of the protein's N-terminal valine. This protein variant is regularly found in diabetic patients, and has been shown to correlate with blood glucose levels. HbA1c's unique chemical properties has made it a reliable marker for diabetes identification and glucose control over 2-3 months (the life span of a red blood cell) [@gallagher2009review]. Given this, hospitals utilize HbA1c measurements to test for glycemic control, as it provides insight into how effective certain diabetes treatments are. Since its popularization in the Diabetes Control & Complications Trial (DCCT), the assay has been internationally standardized under the International Federation of Clinical Chemists (IFCC) [@gallagher2009review].

**Research Question:** Can testing for HbA1c during inpatient visits for individuals with diabetes predict whether the patient will be readmitted within the next month? In other words, is HbA1c measurement an indicator of effective diabetes care?

**Hypothesis:** Given the reliability of the HbA1c test and its insight into diabetes progress, we would expect that patients tested for HbA1c at the hospital would receive more accurate treatment and thus would be less likely to encounter further diabetic complications that would lead them to an early readmission. As such, we would hypothesize that administration of a HbA1c test (regardless of the test result) would lead to delayed readmission or no readmission.

### Data Set 2: Indicators of Heart Disease (2022)

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) develops through a combination of biological, behavioral, and lifestyle factors that accumulate over time. Rather than acting independently, these elements tend to cluster and reinforce one another, influencing overall cardiovascular health. Obesity is one of the most widely studied contributors to this risk and is closely tied to factors such as physical activity, smoking, and other lifestyle habits [@powell2021obesity]. Therefore, understanding its role in cardiovascular health requires considering it within this broader network of influences.

Body mass index (BMI), calculated from an individual's height and weight, is commonly used in research and healthcare as a simple measure of obesity and a proxy for cardiometabolic health. Higher BMI is generally associated with higher probability of cardiovascular conditions, including heart disease and failure [@carbone2022impact]. However, this relationship is not uniform across all populations. Recent research has found that evidence of the "obesity paradox" suggests that in certain contexts, BMI does not always align with expected health outcomes [@tutor2023updates]. This highlights that its meaning depends on underlying health status and related risk factors. As a result, BMI is best understood as an accessible indicator that reflects multiple underlying influences.

Because of this, BMI is most informative when examined alongside behavioral and demographic factors that affect cardiovascular health. Smoking, physical activity, and self-reported health status are all associated with CVD outcomes and help explain differences in BMI across individuals [@powell2021obesity]. These behaviors also tend to co-occur, forming broader patterns of health behavior that influence both weight and long-term disease risk.

The *Indicators of Heart Disease (2022)* data set from Kaggle includes BMI (a continuous variable) alongside demographic characteristics, health behaviors, and self-reported health status, making it well suited for examining the relationship among these components. Accordingly, this study asks how BMI is associated with these behavioral and demographic characteristics.

Based on prior studies, BMI is expected to be higher among individuals who report lower physical activity, poorer general health, and smoking behavior. It is also expected to vary across demographic characteristics such as age, reflecting differences in lifestyle patterns and accumulated health risks over time.
